Encode an R object as JSON (jsonlite's toJSON, natively)

Source: R/json_native.R
tojs.Rd

Converts R data (vectors, lists, data frames, matrices, dates, factors) to JSON text, with the same options, the same defaults and the same bytes out as jsonlite's toJSON(), but computed by this package's own code, so manifests, provenance records and capsules can be written where jsonlite is not installed and their digests stay the same either way. Use it to write data for an API or a person; use jsser() when the JSON must rebuild the exact R object (classes, factor levels, attributes).

Usage

tojs(
  x,
  dataframe = c("rows", "columns", "values"),
  matrix = c("rowmajor", "columnmajor"),
  Date = c("ISO8601", "epoch"),
  POSIXt = c("string", "ISO8601", "epoch", "mongo"),
  factor = c("string", "integer"),
  complex = c("string", "list"),
  raw = c("base64", "hex", "mongo", "int", "js"),
  null = c("list", "null"),
  na = c("null", "string"),
  auto_unbox = FALSE,
  digits = 4,
  pretty = FALSE,
  force = FALSE,
  ...
)

Arguments

x

The object to encode.

dataframe

How a data frame is written: "rows" (the default, an array of records), "columns" (an object of column arrays) or "values" (an array of row arrays, without names).

matrix

How a matrix is written. "rowmajor" (the default) gives an array of rows, and "columnmajor" an array of columns.

Date

How a Date is written: "ISO8601" (the default, "2024-01-02") or "epoch" (days since 1970-01-01).

POSIXt

How a date-time is written: "string" (the default, "2024-01-02 03:04:05"), "ISO8601" ("2024-01-02T03:04:05"), "epoch" (milliseconds since 1970) or "mongo" ({"$date": ms}).

factor

How a factor is written: "string" (the default, its labels) or "integer" (its codes).

complex

How a complex number is written: "string" (the default, "1+2i") or "list" (an object of real and imaginary arrays).

raw

How a raw vector is written: "base64" (the default, one string), "hex", "mongo", "int" or "js".

null

How NULL inside a list is written: "list" (the default, {}; a round trip gives an empty list) or "null" (a JSON null). jsser() round-trips NULL exactly.

na

How missing values are written: "null" or "string" ("NA"). When not given, the per-type default of jsonlite applies (see Details).

auto_unbox

Logical scalar, default FALSE: write length-one vectors as scalars (1) rather than arrays ([1]).

digits

Numeric scalar, default 4: decimal places kept for doubles. I(n) means n significant digits (I(17) writes every double exactly) and NA means 15 significant digits.

pretty

FALSE (the default) for compact output, TRUE to indent by two spaces, or a number of spaces.

force

Logical scalar, default FALSE: write objects that have no JSON form (as {}) instead of failing.

...

Further options of jsonlite's toJSON() and of this package (see Details).

Value

A character scalar of class json, the JSON text.

Details

Atomic vectors become arrays, so a single value is [1] unless auto_unbox = TRUE. Named lists become objects and unnamed lists arrays. Missing values follow jsonlite: with na not given, a missing number is written as the string "NA" and a missing string or logical as null; in a data frame by rows a missing value is left out of its record.

Further options of toJSON() are taken through ...: rownames, keep_vec_names, json_verbatim, always_decimal, time_format, UTC, no_dots, hms ("string" or "secs"), and two of this package's own: keep_empty_names (an empty-string key is written as "" rather than replaced by its position) and quiet_vec_names (no message when keep_vec_names is used). mnfcanon() uses both.

Errors: an option value not among its choices (the message lists them); an object with no JSON form (a function, a symbol) unless force = TRUE.

See also

fromjs() for the reverse, jsser() for an exact round trip.

Examples

tojs(list(a = 1:3, b = "x"), auto_unbox = TRUE)
#> {"a":[1,2,3],"b":"x"} 
tojs(data.frame(id = 1:2, v = c(1.5, NA)), pretty = TRUE)
#> [
#>   {
#>     "id": 1,
#>     "v": 1.5
#>   },
#>   {
#>     "id": 2
#>   }
#> ] 

# a data frame by columns, and a date-time in ISO 8601
df <- data.frame(id = 1:2, v = c(1.5, NA))
tojs(df, dataframe = "columns", na = "null")
#> {"id":[1,2],"v":[1.5,null]} 
tojs(as.POSIXct("2024-01-02 03:04:05", tz = "UTC"), POSIXt = "ISO8601")
#> ["2024-01-02T03:04:05"] 

# digits: decimal places by default, significant digits with I()
tojs(pi)
#> [3.1416] 
tojs(pi, digits = I(17))
#> [3.1415926535897931] 

# a choice that does not exist is refused
try(tojs(df, dataframe = "table"))
#> Error : `dataframe` must be one of "rows", "columns", "values", not "table"
